claim: The ReFRAME library contains approximately 13,000 small molecules that have undergone substantial preclinical evaluation and clinical development or are FDA-approved.
source: This library contains ~13,000 small molecules that have undergone substantial preclinical evaluation and clinical development are FDA-approved (Figure 1A; Janes et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Janes et al., 2018 and reference to Figure 1A showing library composition

claim: SM04690 is a clinical stage inhibitor of CLK2.
source: From a high-throughput chemical screen of the comprehensive drug repurposing library ReFRAME, here we report the identification of SM04690, a clinical stage inhibitor of CLK2, as a potent activator of YAP-driven transcriptional activity in cells.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a characterization of SM04690

claim: CLK2 inhibition promotes alternative splicing of AMOTL2.
source: CLK2 inhibition promotes alternative splicing of the Hippo pathway protein AMOTL2, producing an exon-skipped gene product that can no longer associate with membrane-bound proteins, resulting in decreased phosphorylation and membrane localization of YAP.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study

claim: Exon-skipped AMOTL2 cannot associate with membrane-bound proteins.
source: CLK2 inhibition promotes alternative splicing of the Hippo pathway protein AMOTL2, producing an exon-skipped gene product that can no longer associate with membrane-bound proteins, resulting in decreased phosphorylation and membrane localization of YAP.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a mechanistic consequence of alternative splicing

claim: Alternative splicing of AMOTL2 results in decreased phosphorylation of YAP.
source: CLK2 inhibition promotes alternative splicing of the Hippo pathway protein AMOTL2, producing an exon-skipped gene product that can no longer associate with membrane-bound proteins, resulting in decreased phosphorylation and membrane localization of YAP.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a consequence of AMOTL2 alternative splicing

claim: Alternative splicing of AMOTL2 results in decreased membrane localization of YAP.
source: CLK2 inhibition promotes alternative splicing of the Hippo pathway protein AMOTL2, producing an exon-skipped gene product that can no longer associate with membrane-bound proteins, resulting in decreased phosphorylation and membrane localization of YAP.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a consequence of AMOTL2 alternative splicing

claim: YAP is the downstream effector of the Hippo pathway.
source: Yes-associated protein (YAP), the downstream effector of the evolutionarily conserved Hippo pathway, promotes cellular proliferation and coordinates certain regenerative responses in mammals.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as established knowledge about YAP

claim: YAP promotes cellular proliferation.
source: Yes-associated protein (YAP), the downstream effector of the evolutionarily conserved Hippo pathway, promotes cellular proliferation and coordinates certain regenerative responses in mammals.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a known function of YAP

claim: YAP coordinates certain regenerative responses in mammals.
source: Yes-associated protein (YAP), the downstream effector of the evolutionarily conserved Hippo pathway, promotes cellular proliferation and coordinates certain regenerative responses in mammals.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a known function of YAP

claim: Small molecule activators of YAP may display therapeutic utility in treating disease states involving insufficient proliferative repair.
source: Small molecule activators of YAP may, therefore, display therapeutic utility in treating disease states involving insufficient proliferative repair.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a hypothesis based on YAP's biological functions

claim: MST1 and MST2 phosphorylate and activate LATS1 and LATS2.
source: The core pathway includes Ste20-like kinase 1 (MST1) and MST2, which phosphorylate and activate large tumor suppressor kinase 1 (LATS1) and LATS2 (Wu et al., 2003; Xu et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2003 and Xu et al., 1995

claim: LATS1/2 phosphorylation results in the phosphorylation of YAP, leading to its cytoplasmic retention and inactivation.
source: LATS1/2 phosphorylation results in the phosphorylation of downstream effector Yes-associated protein 1 (YAP), leading to its cytoplasmic retention and inactivation (Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2005

claim: SAV1 binds to MST1/2.
source: Several other proteins work together to regulate the core kinase cascade, such as Salvador homolog 1 (SAV1) and MOB kinase activator 1 A and 1B (MOB1A/B), binders of MST1/2 and LATS1/2, respectively (Udan et al., 2003; Lai et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Udan et al., 2003 and Lai et al., 2005

claim: MOB1A/B binds to LATS1/2.
source: Several other proteins work together to regulate the core kinase cascade, such as Salvador homolog 1 (SAV1) and MOB kinase activator 1 A and 1B (MOB1A/B), binders of MST1/2 and LATS1/2, respectively (Udan et al., 2003; Lai et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Udan et al., 2003 and Lai et al., 2005

claim: AMOT family proteins (AMOT, AMOTL1, and AMOTL2) directly bind to YAP and cause its localization at tight junctions.
source: In addition to phosphorylation-dependent regulation of the Hippo pathway, YAP is also regulated by protein-protein interactions, such as with the angiomotin family of proteins (AMOT, AMOTL1, and AMOTL2), which directly bind to and cause the localization of YAP at tight junctions (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011

claim: When the Hippo pathway is inactivated, YAP translocates to the nucleus.
source: When the Hippo pathway is inactivated, YAP translocates to the nucleus, acting as a transcriptional co-activator of TEA domain transcription factors (TEADs), which increases the transcription of genes involved in cellular proliferation and survival.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about Hippo pathway regulation

claim: Nuclear YAP acts as a transcriptional co-activator of TEAD transcription factors.
source: When the Hippo pathway is inactivated, YAP translocates to the nucleus, acting as a transcriptional co-activator of TEA domain transcription factors (TEADs), which increases the transcription of genes involved in cellular proliferation and survival.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about YAP function

claim: YAP-TEAD interaction increases transcription of genes involved in cellular proliferation and survival.
source: When the Hippo pathway is inactivated, YAP translocates to the nucleus, acting as a transcriptional co-activator of TEA domain transcription factors (TEADs), which increases the transcription of genes involved in cellular proliferation and survival.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about YAP-TEAD function

claim: Hepatic knockdown of MST1/2 with siRNA in mice after partial hepatectomy augments liver regeneration via YAP-dependent hepatocyte proliferation.
source: For example, hepatic knockdown of MST1/2 with small interfering RNA (siRNA) in the mouse after partial hepatectomy augments regeneration of the liver via YAP-dependent hepatocyte proliferation (Loforese et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Loforese et al., 2017

claim: YAP is essential for regenerative wound repair in skin.
source: Likewise, in the skin, YAP is essential for regenerative wound repair, as siRNA-mediated knockdown of YAP markedly delays wound closure (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2014

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of YAP markedly delays wound closure in skin.
source: Likewise, in the skin, YAP is essential for regenerative wound repair, as siRNA-mediated knockdown of YAP markedly delays wound closure (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2014

claim: Conditional hyperactivation of YAP enhances proliferation of epidermal keratinocytes, thickening the epidermal layer of neonatal mice.
source: Conversely, conditional hyperactivation of YAP enhances the proliferation of epidermal keratinocytes, thickening the epidermal layer of neonatal mice (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2011

claim: Conditional SAV deletion in the heart promotes proliferation of cardiomyocytes and reverses deficits in ejection fraction volume post-myocardial infarction.
source: Lastly, in the heart, an organ previously considered to have no regenerative potential post-development, conditional SAV deletion promotes the proliferation of cardiomyocytes and reverses deficits in ejection fraction volume post-myocardial infarction (Leach et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leach et al., 2017

claim: PY-60 activates YAP by binding to annexin A2 (ANXA2).
source: We recently reported the identification of PY-60, a small molecule that activates YAP by binding to a membrane-binding scaffolding protein, annexin A2 (ANXA2), which we defined as a central component of the Hippo pathway (Shalhout et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shalhout et al., 2021

claim: ANXA2 is a central component of the Hippo pathway.
source: We recently reported the identification of PY-60, a small molecule that activates YAP by binding to a membrane-binding scaffolding protein, annexin A2 (ANXA2), which we defined as a central component of the Hippo pathway (Shalhout et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shalhout et al., 2021

claim: SM04690 is in clinical trials for the treatment of osteoarthritis.
source: Among these, we chose to further characterize SM04690, which is in clinical trials for the treatment of osteoarthritis of the knee, as no association of its target kinases had previously been reported as related to Hippo pathway signaling (Deshmukh et al., 2018; Yazici et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deshmukh et al., 2018 and Yazici et al., 2017

claim: Nine kinase inhibitors were identified as reproducible YAP activators from the ReFRAME screen.
source: Evaluating these 15 hits in dose response using the original screening assay with library material, we confirmed nine displayed reproducible YAP activation (Figure 1D).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1D with dose-response curves

claim: Cerdulatinib is an inhibitor of SYK and JAK paralogs with a TEAD-LUC EC50 of 0.31 µM.
source: Of these, three were inhibitors of non-receptor tyrosine kinases including Cerdulatinib (inhibitor of SYK and JAK paralogs Coffey et al., 2014; TEAD-LUC EC50=0.31 µM), Peficitinib (a pan JAK inhibitor Nakada and Oda, 2015; TEAD-LUC EC50=2.4 µM), and KX02 (an inhibitor of SRC family kinases Tu et al., 2012; TEAD-LUC EC50=3.7 µM).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coffey et al., 2014 and experimental data from screening

claim: Peficitinib is a pan JAK inhibitor with a TEAD-LUC EC50 of 2.4 µM.
source: Of these, three were inhibitors of non-receptor tyrosine kinases including Cerdulatinib (inhibitor of SYK and JAK paralogs Coffey et al., 2014; TEAD-LUC EC50=0.31 µM), Peficitinib (a pan JAK inhibitor Nakada and Oda, 2015; TEAD-LUC EC50=2.4 µM), and KX02 (an inhibitor of SRC family kinases Tu et al., 2012; TEAD-LUC EC50=3.7 µM).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakada and Oda, 2015 and experimental data from screening

claim: KX02 is an inhibitor of SRC family kinases with a TEAD-LUC EC50 of 3.7 µM.
source: Of these, three were inhibitors of non-receptor tyrosine kinases including Cerdulatinib (inhibitor of SYK and JAK paralogs Coffey et al., 2014; TEAD-LUC EC50=0.31 µM), Peficitinib (a pan JAK inhibitor Nakada and Oda, 2015; TEAD-LUC EC50=2.4 µM), and KX02 (an inhibitor of SRC family kinases Tu et al., 2012; TEAD-LUC EC50=3.7 µM).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tu et al., 2012 and experimental data from screening

claim: XL-999 is a pan RTK inhibitor with a TEAD-LUC EC50 of 1.5 µM.
source: Also identified as efficacious YAP activators were XL-999 (a pan RTK inhibitor, TEAD-LUC EC50=1.5 µM) and CEP-1347 (a JNK family inhibitor; TEAD-LUC EC50=2.5 µM).
evidence: Stated in text with experimental EC50 value from screening

claim: CEP-1347 is a JNK family inhibitor with a TEAD-LUC EC50 of 2.5 µM.
source: Also identified as efficacious YAP activators were XL-999 (a pan RTK inhibitor, TEAD-LUC EC50=1.5 µM) and CEP-1347 (a JNK family inhibitor; TEAD-LUC EC50=2.5 µM).
evidence: Stated in text with experimental EC50 value from screening

claim: SM04690 activates TEAD-LUC reporter activity with an EC50 of 1.2 nM.
source: We first confirmed the YAP-stimulating activity of SM04690 in 384-well format using 293A-TEAD-LUC cells with fresh, commercially obtained material, finding that the compound dose-dependently increased TEAD-LUC reporter activity with an EC50 of 1.2 nM, a value considerably more potent than that observed in the screening assay (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2A with dose-response curve

claim: SM04690 significantly increases the levels of YAP-controlled transcripts ANKRD1 and CTGF.
source: We next confirmed that SM04690 functionally activated a YAP driven transcriptional program, as SM04690 was found to significantly increase the levels of YAP-controlled transcripts ANKRD1 and CTGF (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2B with RT-qPCR results

claim: SM04690 treatment dose-dependently decreases phosphorylation of YAP.
source: Likewise, SM04690 treatment markedly decreased phosphorylation of YAP, as SM04690 was found to decrease immunopositivity dose-dependently to anti-phospho-YAP in Western blotting experiments following 24 hr compound treatment (Figure 2C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2C with Western blot

claim: SM04690 fails to increase ANKRD1 and CTGF transcript levels in the absence of YAP.
source: We next knocked down YAP transcript using shRNA and found that 1 µM compound treatment failed to increase ANKRD1 and CTGF transcript levels in the absence of YAP, suggesting the compound activates a YAP-dependent transcriptional program (Figure 2D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2D with shRNA knockdown and RT-qPCR

claim: SM04690 treatment promotes nuclear translocation of YAP in MDCK cells.
source: We additionally observed by immunofluorescent imaging that YAP localized to the nucleus in MDCK cells treated with SM04690 (1 µM, 24 hr), suggesting that compound treatment promotes nuclear translocation and activation of YAP. This is in comparison to diffuse plasma membrane and cytoplasm YAP localization in DMSO-treated cells (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figures 2E and 2F with immunofluorescence imaging

claim: 0.2 nM SM04690 treatment promotes clonal expansion of immortalized human keratinocytes (HaCaT) over 7 days.
source: Lastly, since pharmacological YAP activators have been shown to promote the expansion of cells, we tested 0.2 nM SM04690 treatment in immortalized human keratinocytes (HaCaT) over 7 days and found treatment promoted clonal expansion, as seen with rhodamine B staining and increased nuclei counts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: SM04690 was first described as an inhibitor of Wnt signaling capable of promoting differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells to chondrocytes.
source: SM04690 was first described in the literature as an inhibitor of Wnt signaling capable of promoting differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells to chondrocytes (Deshmukh et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deshmukh et al., 2018

claim: SM04690 is an inhibitor of CLK2, CLK3, DYRK1A, DYRK1B, HIPK1, and HIPK2.
source: Specifically, SM04690 has been shown to inhibit CLK2, CLK3, DYRK1A and B, Homeodomain Interacting Protein Kinase 1 (HIPK1), and HIPK2 with over 90% inhibition at 500 nM (Deshmukh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deshmukh et al., 2019

claim: Among the targets of SM04690, only CLK2, DYRK1B, HIPK1, and HIPK2 are expressed in HEK293A cells.
source: Previously published transcript expression data from our lab indicated that among the targets of SM04690 only CLK2, DYRK1B, HIPK1, and HIPK2 are expressed in HEK293A cells, helping to narrow our search (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Shalhout et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shalhout et al., 2021 and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Only inhibitors targeting CLK2 (CC671, CLK-in-T3, and T025) elicited a dose-dependent increase in YAP activity.
source: We found that only inhibitors targeting CLK2 (CC671, CLK-in-T3, and T025) elicited a dose-dependent increase in YAP activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Inhibitors targeting DYRKs (Harmine, INDY, and Leucettine L41) and CLK4 (ML167, TG003) showed no YAP-activating activity.
source: In contrast, inhibitors targeting DYRKs (Harmine, INDY, and Leucettine L41) and CLK4 (ML167, TG003) showed no activity at concentrations over multiple orders of magnitude (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: Knockdown of CLK2 by approximately 50% using three different targeting shRNAs increased YAP-controlled transcripts ANKRD1, CTGF, and CYR61.
source: To confirm CLK2 as the relevant target of SM04690, we knocked down CLK2 by approximately 50% using three different targeting shRNAs, all of which increased YAP-controlled transcripts ANKRD1, CTGF, and CYR61 to varying degrees (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B with shRNA knockdown and RT-qPCR

claim: CLK2 is a protein kinase that phosphorylates serine/arginine-rich (SR) proteins of the spliceosomal complex.
source: CLK2 is a protein kinase that phosphorylates serine/arginine-rich (SR) proteins of the spliceosomal complex, which play an important role in exon selection by the spliceosome (Jeong, 2017; Long and Caceres, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jeong, 2017 and Long and Caceres, 2009

claim: The phosphorylation states of SR proteins dictate their subcellular localization and interactions with pre-mRNA.
source: The phosphorylation states of SR proteins dictate their subcellular localization and interactions with pre-mRNA (da Silva et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to da Silva et al., 2015

claim: When CLK2 is inhibited, SR proteins are not phosphorylated, leading to alternative splicing that is most often exon skipping.
source: When CLK2 is inhibited, SR proteins are not phosphorylated, leading to alternative splicing that is most often exon skipping (Salvador and Gomis, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Salvador and Gomis, 2018

claim: Exon 5 of AMOTL2 is the third most skipped exon of the transcriptome in response to CLK2 inhibition.
source: Interestingly, the third most skipped exon of the transcriptome in response to CLK2 inhibition corresponded to exon 5 of Angiomotin-like 2 (AMOTL2), as nearly 3,000 new junction reads between non-neighboring exons were observed in this study (Araki et al., 2015; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by citation to Araki et al., 2015 and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Exon 9 of AMOTL2 is also skipped in response to CLK2 inhibition but to a lesser extent than exon 5.
source: Exon 9 of AMOTL2 was also skipped but to a lesser extent with around 700 new junction reads.
evidence: Stated in text based on data from Araki et al., 2015

claim: AMOTL2 interacts with YAP's WW domain.
source: AMOTL2 is part of the AMOT family of proteins and is crucial to the tight junction localization of YAP through direct interaction with YAP's WW domain (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011

claim: Knockdown of AMOTL2 decreases tight junction-localized YAP and promotes YAP translocation to the nucleus.
source: Notably, the knockdown of AMOTL2 decreases the content of tight junction-localized YAP, instead promoting YAP translocation to the nucleus (Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2011

claim: 24 hr SM04690 treatment at 1 µM induces exon 5 skipping of AMOTL2 by 629-fold.
source: Consistent with reported literature, quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) revealed that 24 hr SM04690 treatment at 1 µM induces exon skipping for exon 5 by 629-fold and exon 9 by 80-fold when compared to untreated samples (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B

claim: 24 hr SM04690 treatment at 1 µM induces exon 9 skipping of AMOTL2 by 80-fold.
source: Consistent with reported literature, quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) revealed that 24 hr SM04690 treatment at 1 µM induces exon skipping for exon 5 by 629-fold and exon 9 by 80-fold when compared to untreated samples (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B

claim: Exon skipping of AMOTL2 exons 5 and 9 is observed at concentrations as low as 10 nM SM04690 with 24 hr treatment.
source: The skipping of exons 5 and 9 was observed as low as 10 nM with 24 hr treatment of SM04690 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A

claim: SM04690 treatment increases the total AMOTL2 transcript level by 2.3-fold.
source: It is important to note that both the RT-qPCR and Western blot not only indicate the increase in alternative splicing but also an increase in the total AMOTL2 present with SM04690 treatment, as the relative transcript level of total AMOTL2 in SM04690 treated cells increased 2.3-fold in the RT-qPCR analysis and the Western blot showed increase bandwidth.
evidence: Experimental data from RT-qPCR and Western blot analyses

claim: The three AMOTL2 spliceoforms (∆5, ∆9, ∆5∆9) retain a similar ability to bind YAP as wild-type AMOTL2.
source: We found that the three AMOTL2 spliceoforms retained a similar ability to bind YAP as the WT AMOTL2 transgene (Figure 3E).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3E with co-immunoprecipitation

claim: AMOTL2 ∆5∆9 displays 1.5-2 times higher levels of YAP-controlled transcripts compared to wild-type AMOTL2 overexpression.
source: From experiments in HEK293A cells transiently overexpressing WT AMOLT2 or each of the three transgenes (AMOTL2 ∆5, AMOTL2 ∆9, AMOTL2 ∆5∆9), AMOTL2 ∆5∆9 uniquely displayed 1.5–2 times higher levels of YAP controlled transcripts in comparison to cell overexpressing WT AMOTL2 (Figure 3F).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3F with RT-qPCR

claim: Overexpression of wild-type AMOTL2 inhibits the upregulation of ANKRD1, CTGF, and CYR61 in response to 20 nM SM04690 treatment.
source: Indeed, overexpression of WT AMOTL2 was found to inhibit the upregulation of ANKRD1, CTGF, and CYR61 in response to 20 nM compound treatment (Figure 3G), indicating that inducing alternative splicing is essential to the mechanism of SM04690.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3G with RT-qPCR

claim: AMOTL2 localizes to tight junctions at the plasma membrane of MDCK cells in conditions of high cell density.
source: Consistent with previous research on the subcellular localization of AMOT family proteins (Zhao et al., 2011; Wells et al., 2006; Mana-Capelli et al., 2014), we found that AMOTL2 localizes to tight junctions at the plasma membrane of MDCK cells in conditions of high cell density (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B with immunofluorescence, supported by citations

claim: 1 µM SM04690 treatment for 24 hr in MDCK cells results in AMOTL2 being less efficiently localized to the plasma membrane.
source: Interestingly, we found that when MDCK cells were plated at high density and then treated with 1 µM SM04690 for 24 hr, AMOTL2 was much less efficiently localized to the plasma membrane as assessed by immunofluorescent staining followed by confocal microscopy (Figure 4A).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4A with immunofluorescence imaging

claim: SM04690 treatment results in greater than twofold loss of colocalization of AMOTL2 with E-cadherin.
source: Indeed, SM04690-treated samples displayed a greater than twofold loss of colocalization of AMOTL2 with adherens junction protein E-cadherin (Figure 4B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4B with quantification of colocalization

claim: 1 µM SM04690 treatment results in a 10-fold increase in AMOTL2 puncta in HEK293A cells.
source: This effect on AMOTL2 puncta formation could be additionally recapitulated in HEK293A cells (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), as 1 µM SM04690 resulted in a 10-fold increase in puncta.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: Overexpression of AMOTL2 ∆5∆9 in HEK293A cells displays over 10-fold increases in puncta compared to wild-type AMOTL2.
source: Likewise, we found that overexpression of AMOTL2 ∆5, AMOTL2 ∆9, and AMOTL2 ∆5∆9 in HEK293A cells displayed dramatic increases in puncta number in comparison to WT AMOTL2 expression, with over 10-fold increases in puncta for AMOTL2 ∆5∆9 compared to WT AMOTL2 (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: 1 µM SM04690 treatment for 24 hr decreases colocalization of AMOTL2 with PALS1 by approximately twofold.
source: Indeed, co-immunofluorescent studies in MDCK cells plated at high density indicated that 1 µM SM04690 treatment for 24 hr decreases co-localization of AMOTL2 with PALS1 and MAGI1 by approximately twofold (Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figures 4E, 4F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B

claim: 1 µM SM04690 treatment for 24 hr decreases colocalization of AMOTL2 with MAGI1 by approximately twofold.
source: Indeed, co-immunofluorescent studies in MDCK cells plated at high density indicated that 1 µM SM04690 treatment for 24 hr decreases co-localization of AMOTL2 with PALS1 and MAGI1 by approximately twofold (Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figures 4E, 4F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B

claim: AMOTL2 ∆9 and AMOTL2 ∆5∆9 lose their ability to interact with the WW domain regions of MAGI1.
source: From co-immunoprecipitation with the FLAG-tagged AMOTL2 spliceoforms in HEK293T cells, we found that AMOTL2 ∆9 and AMOTL2 ∆5∆9 lost their ability to interact with the WW domain regions of MAGI1 (Figure 4G).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4G with co-immunoprecipitation

claim: AMOTL2 was originally discovered as an interactor of MAGI1.
source: AMOTL2 was originally discovered as an interactor of the membrane-associated protein Membrane Associated Guanylate Kinase, WW, and PDZ Domain Containing 1 (MAGI1), and it has also been shown to interact with tight junction-associated proteins such as Protein Associated with LIN7, MAGUK p55 Family Member (PALS1) (Patrie, 2005; Ernkvist et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Patrie, 2005 and Ernkvist et al., 2009

claim: AMOTL2 interacts with tight junction-associated protein PALS1.
source: AMOTL2 was originally discovered as an interactor of the membrane-associated protein Membrane Associated Guanylate Kinase, WW, and PDZ Domain Containing 1 (MAGI1), and it has also been shown to interact with tight junction-associated proteins such as Protein Associated with LIN7, MAGUK p55 Family Member (PALS1) (Patrie, 2005; Ernkvist et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Patrie, 2005 and Ernkvist et al., 2009

claim: AMOTL2 localizes YAP to tight junctions through interactions with membrane-associated proteins.
source: Through these interactions, AMOTL2 localizes YAP to tight junctions, where YAP is inactivated by phosphorylation.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge based on previous research

claim: AMOTL2 serves a central role in regulating the Hippo pathway.
source: AMOTL2 serves a central role in regulating the Hippo pathway.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section

claim: AMOTL2 inhibits YAP by restraining it to the plasma membrane while concurrently stimulating the enzymatic activity of LATS1/2.
source: Specifically, AMOTL2 has been shown to inhibit YAP, restraining it to the plasma membrane while concurrently stimulating the enzymatic activity of LATS1/2 (Paramasivam et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paramasivam et al., 2011

claim: AMOTL2 acts as a scaffolding protein, bringing LATS1/2 in close proximity to MST1/2 at the plasma membrane.
source: These functions are possible due to AMOTL2's activity as a scaffolding protein, bringing LATS1/2 in close proximity to MST1/2 at the plasma membrane (Mana-Capelli and McCollum, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mana-Capelli and McCollum, 2018

claim: Overexpression of wild-type AMOTL2 attenuates transcription of YAP-controlled genes in the context of SM04690 treatment.
source: The work presented here adds to the mounting evidence that AMOTL2 acts as a negative regulator of YAP, most prominently displayed through an attenuation of transcription of YAP-controlled genes when wild-type AMOTL2 is overexpressed in the context of the YAP-activating compound SM04690 (Figure 3G).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: AMOT regulates Hippo pathway activity through the formation of biomolecular condensates.
source: It has been shown that the AMOTL2-related protein AMOT regulates Hippo pathway activity through the formation of biomolecular condensates, in contrast to traditional scaffolding proteins (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2022

claim: AMOT-laden condensates concentrate core Hippo pathway kinases and potentially sequester YAP in the cytoplasm.
source: AMOT-laden condensates have been shown to concentrate core Hippo pathway kinases, acting to potentially sequester YAP in the cytoplasm.
evidence: Stated based on previous research on AMOT condensates

claim: There is considerable redundancy between AMOT and AMOTL2.
source: Since there is considerable redundancy between AMOT and AMOTL2 (Mana-Capelli and McCollum, 2018; Li et al., 2012; Hirate and Sasaki, 2014; Leung and Zernicka-Goetz, 2013), it is conceivable that AMOTL2 may also regulate YAP through biomolecular condensates.
evidence: Supported by citations to Mana-Capelli and McCollum, 2018; Li et al., 2012; Hirate and Sasaki, 2014; Leung and Zernicka-Goetz, 2013

claim: YAP has eight different isoforms due to tissue-specific alternative splicing.
source: For example, tissue-specific alternative splicing of YAP itself can lead to eight different isoforms and has been shown to regulate its activity by altering the efficiency with which it interacts with LATS1/2 and TEADs, leading to cell-type specific effects on cellular proliferation (Gaffney et al., 2012; Iglesias-Bexiga et al., 2015; Vrbský et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gaffney et al., 2012; Iglesias-Bexiga et al., 2015; Vrbský et al., 2021

claim: LATS1 exists as 7 spliceoforms in the cell.
source: In addition, LATS1 and LATS2 exist as 7 and 2 spliceoforms in the cell, respectively, affecting their interactions with Hippo pathway scaffolding proteins Neurofibromin 2 (NF2) and MOB1 and modulating their catalytic activity (Porazinski and Ladomery, 2018; Kulaberoglu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Porazinski and Ladomery, 2018; Kulaberoglu et al., 2017

claim: LATS2 exists as 2 spliceoforms in the cell.
